rationale: The unit opens the words-of-the-wise collection with a double attention-imperative, הַ֥ט אָזְנְךָ֗ (oshb:Prov.22.17, 'turn your ear'), paired with וּ֭שְׁמַע (oshb:Prov.22.17, 'and listen'), and the phrase דִּבְרֵ֣י חֲכָמִ֑ים (oshb:Prov.22.17, 'words of the wise') sits mid-verse rather than as a separate header line, so the seam is argued from the clause itself and not from a title. Verse 19 states the address's purpose in an infinitive clause, לִהְי֣וֹת בַּ֭יהוָה (oshb:Prov.22.19, 'so that your trust may be in Yahweh'), and verses 20-21 restate that purpose with two further purpose infinitives, לְהוֹדִֽיעֲךָ֗ and לְהָשִׁ֥יב (oshb:Prov.22.21). The unit closes with a petuchah/pe seg (oshb:Prov.22.21, single-witness), corroborating the move into the content admonitions that open at 22:22. Verse 20 itself carries an unresolved ketiv/qere crux: the consonantal ketiv שלשום against the pointed qere שָׁלִישִׁ֑ים (oshb:Prov.22.20, ketiv/qere, single-witness) leaves the numeral/rank term underlying 'thirty' versus an officer-class reading undecided by the bytes; this row reports the crux without resolving it.
rejected_alternative: Reading 22:17 as a bare title line parallel to the mishle headers was set aside because the divrei-hakhamim wording sits inside the sentence's own grammar, not in a superscription position.
observed_substrate_signals: a double attention-imperative opens the address (Prov.22.17)
a purpose-infinitive clause names Yahweh as the address's goal (Prov.22.19)
two further purpose infinitives restate that goal (Prov.22.21)
petuchah/pe seg at the close (Prov.22.21, single-witness)
a ketiv/qere pair at the numeral/rank term is left unresolved (Prov.22.20, single-witness)
device_notes: The five verses build one periodic sentence (imperative, then three purpose clauses) rather than antithetic couplets, a texture distinct from the sentence-literature run that follows in 23:1 onward.

rationale: A fresh imperative pair opens the verse, אַֽל תִּגְזָל (oshb:Prov.22.22, 'do not rob/exploit the poor'), directly after the petuchah/pe close of the prologue (oshb:Prov.22.21, single-witness); the topic itself changes from the collection's own purpose to a concrete social prohibition, marking the start of a new unit rather than a continuation. Verse 23 supplies the grounding motive with כִּֽי (oshb:Prov.22.23, 'for Yahweh will plead their case'), the standard imperative-plus-motive shape.
rejected_alternative: Folding this pair into the prologue was rejected since the prologue's own purpose clauses end at 22:21 and this couplet opens a distinct social-ethics topic.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition opens the couplet (Prov.22.22)
a motive clause closes it (Prov.22.23)
petuchah/pe at the immediately preceding verse (Prov.22.21, single-witness)
device_notes: Antithetic-free synthetic couplet: command then divine-agency rationale, not a but-contrast.

rationale: אַל תִּ֭תְרַע (oshb:Prov.22.24, 'do not befriend a hot-tempered man') opens a new prohibition unrelated to the court-justice topic just closed; verse 25 supplies a purpose clause, פֶּן תֶּאֱלַ֥ף (oshb:Prov.22.25, 'lest you learn his ways'), completing a two-verse imperative-plus-purpose unit. Verse 25 also carries a ketiv/qere note: the ketiv reads ארחתו against the qere אֹֽרְחֹתָ֑יו (oshb:Prov.22.25, ketiv/qere, single-witness).
rejected_alternative: Extending the unit to include 22:26 was set aside because the surety-pledge topic at 22:26 shares no root with the hot-tempered-companion warning.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition opens the pair (Prov.22.24)
a purpose clause closes it (Prov.22.25)
a ketiv/qere pair at the closing verb (Prov.22.25, single-witness)
device_notes: Synthetic couplet built on prohibition plus consequence, addressed in second person in both verses.

rationale: אַל תְּהִ֥י (oshb:Prov.22.26, 'do not be one of those who strike hands') prohibits standing surety; verse 27 supplies the grounding case as a rhetorical question rather than a motive clause, אִם אֵֽין ...לָ֥מָּה (oshb:Prov.22.27, 'if you have nothing to pay, why should he take your bed'), functioning as the unit's motive in the surety scenario.
rejected_alternative: Treating 22:27 as a separate one-verse proverb was set aside because its rhetorical question draws its force from the surety prohibition it explains rather than standing on its own.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition against striking hands opens the pair (Prov.22.26)
a rhetorical question supplies the motive in place of a plain clause (Prov.22.27)
device_notes: Synthetic pair: command then illustrative consequence-question, the surety theme's own micro-unit.

rationale: אַל תַּ֭סֵּג גְּב֣וּל עוֹלָ֑ם (oshb:Prov.22.28, 'do not move the ancient boundary stone') forms a complete maxim closed by a relative clause naming the fathers who set the boundary; the verse contains no motive clause of its own, which distinguishes it from the imperative-plus-motive shape used for the surrounding admonition_unit rows. The same core prohibition recurs with an added motive at Prov.23.10-Prov.23.11, a non-adjacent restatement rather than a continuation of this verse.
rejected_alternative: Reading this line as an admonition_unit opener continuing into 22:29 was rejected since 22:29 shifts to an unrelated observation about skilled workers, sharing no vocabulary with the boundary-stone maxim.
observed_substrate_signals: a bare prohibition lacking an attached motive clause (Prov.22.28)
the same boundary-stone wording recurs at 23:10 with a motive clause added there
device_notes: A bare imperative maxim rather than an argued admonition; the relative clause names the fathers, not a rationale.

rationale: חָזִ֡יתָ (oshb:Prov.22.29, 'do you see...') opens a rhetorical question about a skilled worker rather than issuing a command, so the verse reads as an observation offered for reflection, not as a second-person prohibition. A petuchah/pe seg follows the verse (oshb:Prov.22.29, single-witness), corroborating the move into the eating-with-a-ruler scene that opens chapter 23.
rejected_alternative: Grouping this verse with 23:1 as one unit about court conduct was set aside because the addressee and grammar change from a third-person observation to a second-person scene-imperative.
observed_substrate_signals: a rhetorical question opens the verse, not an imperative (Prov.22.29)
petuchah/pe seg closes the verse (Prov.22.29, single-witness)
device_notes: Observational proverb built on a skill-before-kings image, distinct in mood from the imperative admonitions on either side.

rationale: A new scene opens with כִּֽי תֵ֭שֵׁב (oshb:Prov.23.1, 'when you sit to eat with a ruler'), immediately after the petuchah/pe seg at the close of 22:29 (oshb:Prov.22.29, single-witness); the imperative תָּ֝בִ֗ין (oshb:Prov.23.1) governs verses 1-2, and verse 3 closes with an explicit prohibition and motive, אַל תִּ֭תְאָו (oshb:Prov.23.3, 'do not desire') ... כְּזָבִֽים (oshb:Prov.23.3, 'deceptive food').
rejected_alternative: Splitting verse 2's knife-at-the-throat image into its own row was rejected because its grammatical subject depends on the eating scene verse 1 sets up rather than standing independently.
observed_substrate_signals: a protasis opens the scene (Prov.23.1)
a prohibition-plus-motive closes it (Prov.23.3)
petuchah/pe at the immediately preceding verse (Prov.22.29, single-witness)
device_notes: One developing scene (protasis, caution, motive) rather than three loose couplets.

rationale: אַל תִּיגַ֥ע לְֽהַעֲשִׁ֑יר (oshb:Prov.23.4, 'do not weary yourself to be rich') opens a new topic distinct from the ruler's table; verse 5 grounds the prohibition with כִּ֤י (oshb:Prov.23.5) and the image of riches sprouting eagle's wings, כְּ֝נֶ֗שֶׁר (oshb:Prov.23.5). Verse 5 carries a ketiv/qere pair at both its verbs, התעוף/הֲתָ֤עִיף and ועיף/יָע֥וּף (oshb:Prov.23.5, ketiv/qere, single-witness), and a petuchah/pe seg follows the verse (oshb:Prov.23.5, petuchah/pe, single-witness).
rejected_alternative: Keeping this pair joined to the preceding table scene was rejected since wealth-that-vanishes is a distinct image, sharing no lexical link with eating before a ruler.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition opens the pair (Prov.23.4)
a motive clause with the eagle-wings image (Prov.23.5)
a ketiv/qere pair at both verbs of verse 5 (Prov.23.5, single-witness)
petuchah/pe seg closes the pair (Prov.23.5, single-witness)
device_notes: Synthetic couplet: prohibition then a vivid simile-motive, the wing image doing the argumentative work a plain motive clause usually carries alone.

rationale: The unit opens right after the petuchah/pe seg at 23:5 (oshb:Prov.23.5, single-witness) with אַל תִּלְחַ֗ם (oshb:Prov.23.6, 'do not eat the bread of a stingy-eyed man'), a return to a table scene distinct from the wealth-warning just closed; verse 6 carries its own ketiv/qere note at its closing verb, תתאו/תִּ֝תְאָ֗יו (oshb:Prov.23.6, ketiv/qere, single-witness). Verse 7 supplies the motive with כִּ֤י (oshb:Prov.23.7, 'for as he reckons the cost, so he is'), and verse 8 gives the resulting consequence, completing a three-verse scene parallel in shape to 23:1-3.
rejected_alternative: Merging this scene with the ruler's-table unit at 23:1-3 was set aside since the two hosts (ruler, stingy man) are named separately and no catchword bridges the wealth-warning couplet between them.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition opens the scene, with a ketiv/qere note (Prov.23.6, single-witness)
a motive clause at verse 7 (Prov.23.7)
a consequence verse closes at 23:8
petuchah/pe at the immediately preceding verse (Prov.23.5, single-witness)
device_notes: A second table-scene admonition_unit, structurally paired with 23:1-3 but kept as its own row since the two scenes name different hosts.

rationale: The verse packs a full imperative-plus-motive shape into one line: בְּאָזְנֵ֣י כְ֭סִיל אַל תְּדַבֵּ֑ר (oshb:Prov.23.9, 'do not speak in a fool's ears') followed in the same verse by כִּֽי (oshb:Prov.23.9, 'for he will despise the wisdom of your words'), so the row treats it as a compressed one-verse admonition_unit rather than a bare maxim.
rejected_alternative: Classifying the verse as a single_proverb was considered, since many one-verse rows in this span carry that label, but the internal motive clause gives it the fuller command-plus-motive shape reserved for admonition_unit.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition and its motive clause both fall inside one verse (Prov.23.9)
device_notes: A miniature of the two-verse admonition pattern compressed into one line; no vocative or catchword ties it to its neighbors.

rationale: אַל תַּ֭סֵּג גְּב֣וּל עוֹלָ֑ם (oshb:Prov.23.10) repeats the boundary-stone wording of Prov.22.28 and adds a second prohibition about the fields of orphans in the same verse; verse 11 supplies the motive this time, כִּֽי גֹאֲלָ֥ם חָזָ֑ק (oshb:Prov.23.11, 'for their defender is strong'), completing the two-verse unit that 22:28 left without one.
rejected_alternative: Reading 23:10-11 as a continuation of the 22:28 row was rejected because the two sit four verses apart with an intervening scene change, so the repeated wording argues restatement rather than one uninterrupted span.
observed_substrate_signals: the boundary-stone prohibition repeats from 22:28, now with a motive clause attached (Prov.23.10, Prov.23.11)
device_notes: A fuller restatement of the boundary-stone maxim, now built out to the imperative-plus-motive shape.

rationale: הָבִ֣יאָה לַמּוּסָ֣ר לִבֶּ֑ךָ (oshb:Prov.23.12, 'apply your heart to discipline') is a second-person command lacking a motive clause, addressed generally rather than to a named scenario. The root under לַמּוּסָ֣ר (oshb:Prov.23.12) recurs at the opening of the child-discipline pair in Prov.23.13, a shared root that could argue for reading the two together; this row treats 23:12 as its own line because it names no child and no rod, keeping the general call to attention separate from the specific application that follows.
rejected_alternative: Folding 23:12 into the 23:13-14 rod-discipline pair as one three-verse unit was considered, since both share the same root, but was set aside because that is one repeated root rather than a fuller run of shared vocabulary.
observed_substrate_signals: a command lacking a motive clause (Prov.23.12)
the same root recurs at the opening of 23:13
device_notes: Functions as a general call-to-attention parallel in kind to 22:17 and 23:19, rather than as a proverb content-line.

rationale: אַל תִּמְנַ֣ע מִנַּ֣עַר מוּסָ֑ר (oshb:Prov.23.13, 'do not withhold discipline from a child') opens with a prohibition and its own motive in the same verse, כִּֽי...יָמֽוּת (oshb:Prov.23.13); verse 14 restates the command positively with אַ֭תָּה בַּשֵּׁ֣בֶט תַּכֶּ֑נּוּ (oshb:Prov.23.14) and adds a second purpose clause about saving the child's life from Sheol, closing a tight two-verse unit on corporal discipline.
rejected_alternative: Reading 23:14 as its own single_proverb was rejected because its imperative restates verse 13's prohibition rather than opening an independent topic.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition and its motive clause fall within verse 13 (Prov.23.13)
a positive restatement plus a second purpose clause closes verse 14 (Prov.23.14)
device_notes: Prohibition-then-positive-restatement shape, the rod-and-child image binding the two verses.

rationale: The vocative בְּ֭נִי (oshb:Prov.23.15, 'my son') opens a new address distinct from the rod-discipline command just closed; the conditional אִם חָכַ֣ם לִבֶּ֑ךָ (oshb:Prov.23.15, 'if your heart is wise') is answered by the father's own joy, and verse 16 restates that joy with וְתַעְלֹ֥זְנָה (oshb:Prov.23.16), closing the two-verse unit before a fresh vocative reopens at 23:19.
rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through 23:18 was set aside because the fear-Yahweh admonition beginning at 23:17 opens its own prohibition and motive rather than continuing the conditional joy-statement of 23:15-16.
observed_substrate_signals: a vocative opens the address (Prov.23.15)
a conditional is answered by the father's joy, restated at verse 16 (Prov.23.15, Prov.23.16)
device_notes: A first-person father-speech unit rather than a second-person prohibition; synthetic parallelism (condition, then joy, then intensified restatement).

rationale: אַל יְקַנֵּ֣א לִ֭בְּךָ (oshb:Prov.23.17, 'do not let your heart envy sinners') opens a fresh prohibition after the father's-joy unit closes at 23:16; the same verse supplies its own contrastive motive, כִּ֥י אִם (oshb:Prov.23.17, 'but rather fear Yahweh'), and verse 18 closes with a hope clause, וְ֝תִקְוָתְךָ֗ לֹ֣א תִכָּרֵֽת (oshb:Prov.23.18, 'your hope will not be cut off'); the same wording recurs at Prov.24.13-Prov.24.14, a non-adjacent refrain rather than a device local to this pair.
rejected_alternative: Treating verse 18 as a detached single_proverb about future hope was rejected because its subject depends on the envy prohibition verse 17 states rather than standing on its own.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition-plus-contrast falls within verse 17 (Prov.23.17)
a hope clause closes verse 18, the same wording recurring at 24:14 (Prov.23.18)
device_notes: The hope-not-cut-off clause is a book-internal refrain (23:18 and 24:13-14 share the exact wording); noted here as texture, not as a boundary argument for either row.

rationale: A second vocative address opens the unit, שְׁמַע אַתָּ֣ה בְנִ֣י (oshb:Prov.23.19, 'listen, you, my son'), distinct from the 23:15 vocative by its own topic (right paths, then drunkenness); verse 20 issues the prohibition אַל תְּהִ֥י בְסֹֽבְאֵי יָ֑יִן (oshb:Prov.23.20, 'do not be among winebibbers'), and verse 21 supplies the motive with כִּי (oshb:Prov.23.21, 'for the drunkard and glutton will grow poor'), closing a three-verse vocative-plus-motive unit.
rejected_alternative: Reading 23:19 as a continuation of the 23:15-16 address was rejected because a fresh vocative reopens the address and the topic moves from filial joy to wine and meat.
observed_substrate_signals: a vocative reopens the address (Prov.23.19)
a prohibition against drunkenness follows (Prov.23.20)
a motive clause closes the unit (Prov.23.21)
device_notes: Vocative-opened admonition_unit; the drunkard/glutton pairing anticipates the fuller wine poem beginning at 23:29.

rationale: שְׁמַ֣ע לְ֭אָבִיךָ (oshb:Prov.23.22, 'listen to your father') opens a paired positive-and-negative command about parents, closed within the same verse by a motive clause, כִּֽי זָקְנָ֥ה (oshb:Prov.23.22, 'for she is old'). The topic (parents) does not continue the drunkenness warning just closed, and 23:23's command to buy truth opens a distinct topic after it, so the verse stands as its own compressed unit.
rejected_alternative: Grouping this verse with 23:24-25's father's-joy couplet was set aside because an unrelated verse on buying truth sits between them, and no root repeats across the gap.
observed_substrate_signals: a paired command about parents with an internal motive clause (Prov.23.22)
device_notes: Command-plus-motive compressed to one verse, matching the shape used for 23:9.

rationale: אֱמֶ֣ת קְ֭נֵה וְאַל תִּמְכֹּ֑ר (oshb:Prov.23.23, 'buy the truth, and do not sell it') stands as a complete merchant-metaphor maxim lacking a motive clause and sharing no vocabulary with either the honor-your-parents command before it or the father's-joy couplet after it.
rejected_alternative: Reading the verse as an admonition_unit on the strength of its imperative form alone was set aside since it lacks the motive clause that distinguishes the fuller command-plus-rationale rows in this span.
observed_substrate_signals: a buy-do-not-sell maxim lacking a motive clause (Prov.23.23)
device_notes: A self-contained commercial-metaphor maxim (buy/do not sell) rather than an argued admonition.

rationale: Verse 24 carries four ketiv/qere pairs in one line -- גול/גִּ֣יל, יגול/יָ֭גִיל, יולד/וְיוֹלֵ֥ד, וישמח/יִשְׂמַח (oshb:Prov.23.24, ketiv/qere, single-witness) -- and its qere verb יִשְׂמַח recurs at the head of verse 25, יִֽשְׂמַח אָבִ֥יךָ וְאִמֶּ֑ךָ (oshb:Prov.23.25, 'let your father and mother be glad'), the shared root binding the general maxim about a righteous child's parent to its applied wish for this son's own parents.
rejected_alternative: Reading verse 24 alone as the row and verse 25 as a separate single_proverb was considered, given the topical shift from general maxim to direct wish, but was set aside because the repeated root binds the two into one developing statement.
observed_substrate_signals: four ketiv/qere pairs sit in one verse (Prov.23.24, single-witness)
the qere verb at 23:24 recurs as the opening verb of 23:25
device_notes: Synthetic pair: general maxim, then its personalized application, joined by a repeated root; the K/Q density leaves the exact wording of verse 24 less certain than the boundary decision itself.

rationale: A third vocative opens the unit, תְּנָֽה בְנִ֣י לִבְּךָ֣ לִ֑י (oshb:Prov.23.26, 'give me your heart, my son'), carrying its own ketiv/qere note, תרצנה/תִּצֹּֽרְנָה (oshb:Prov.23.26, ketiv/qere, single-witness); verse 27 supplies the motive with כִּֽי (oshb:Prov.23.27) and the deep-pit/narrow-well image for the unfaithful wife, and verse 28 continues that image, closing a three-verse vocative-plus-motive unit that reads as the collection's compressed version of the strange-woman warnings developed at length in chapters 1-9.
rejected_alternative: Stopping the unit at verse 26 alone was rejected because the motive clause of verse 27 supplies the rationale the vocative command needs, and verse 28 continues rather than restarts that image.
observed_substrate_signals: a vocative and imperative open the unit, with a ketiv/qere note (Prov.23.26, single-witness)
a motive clause with the deep-pit image follows (Prov.23.27)
device_notes: A vocative-plus-motive admonition on the strange woman, structurally the same shape as 23:19-21 but on a different topic.

rationale: Seven verses build one extended treatment rather than a chain of couplets: verse 29 opens with a six-fold rhetorical לְמִ֨י (oshb:Prov.23.29, 'who has...?') list naming woe, sorrow, and wounds; verse 30 answers the riddle (those who linger over wine); verse 31 supplies the span's one plain imperative, אַל תֵּ֥רֶא יַיִן֮ (oshb:Prov.23.31, 'do not look at the wine'), itself carrying a ketiv/qere pair, בכיס/בַּכּ֣וֹס (oshb:Prov.23.31, ketiv/qere, single-witness); and verses 32-35 describe the aftermath in extended imagery, closing with the drunkard's own quoted words at verse 35. The riddle-form opening and the closing quoted speech mark this as a poem rather than an imperative admonition stretched past its usual two-to-four-verse span.
rejected_alternative: Segmenting the span into shorter admonition_unit rows (29-30, 31, 32-35) was considered but rejected because the six-fold riddle of verse 29 is answered across the full span, not resolved within any short sub-unit.
observed_substrate_signals: a six-fold rhetorical list opens the span (Prov.23.29)
the span's one plain imperative sits at verse 31, itself K/Q-marked (Prov.23.31, single-witness)
the drunkard's own quoted speech closes the span at verse 35
device_notes: Riddle-question opening, descriptive middle, first-person quoted close -- the formal shape recognized elsewhere in the book's set-piece poems, here on drunkenness; chapter boundaries fall cleanly on both sides.

rationale: The chapter opens with אַל תְּ֭קַנֵּא בְּאַנְשֵׁ֣י רָעָ֑ה (oshb:Prov.24.1, 'do not envy evil men'), a fresh topic after the wine poem closes at 23:35, carrying its own ketiv/qere note, תתאו/תִּ֝תְאָ֗יו (oshb:Prov.24.1, ketiv/qere, single-witness); verse 2 supplies the motive with כִּי (oshb:Prov.24.2, 'for their hearts plot violence'). The same verb root recurs at Prov.24.19, a non-adjacent bracketing of the chapter's opening and closing prohibitions rather than a link within this pair.
rejected_alternative: Extending the unit to include verse 3's wisdom-builds-a-house maxim was rejected because verse 3 shares no root with the envy prohibition and opens a distinct declarative topic.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition opens the chapter, with a ketiv/qere note (Prov.24.1, single-witness)
a motive clause follows at verse 2 (Prov.24.2)
the same verb root recurs at 24:19, bracketing the chapter's open with a later prohibition rather than binding to this pair
device_notes: Standard prohibition-plus-motive shape; the recurrence of the envy-verb at 24:19 is noted as texture, not as grounds to widen this row.

rationale: בְּ֭חָכְמָה יִבָּ֣נֶה בָּ֑יִת (oshb:Prov.24.3, 'through wisdom a house is built') opens a declarative image rather than an imperative; verse 4 continues the same house image with חֲדָרִ֣ים (oshb:Prov.24.4, 'rooms... filled'), the shared building-image vocabulary (house, established, rooms) binding the pair as one developing figure rather than two unrelated maxims.
rejected_alternative: Reading verses 3 and 4 as two separate single_proverb rows was set aside because verse 4's rooms-filled-with-treasure image completes rather than restarts the house-building figure verse 3 opens.
observed_substrate_signals: a house-building image opens the pair (Prov.24.3)
the same image continues at verse 4 (rooms filled with treasure)
device_notes: Declarative synthetic pair, no imperative; wisdom's practical benefit shown through the house figure.

rationale: גֶּֽבֶר חָכָ֥ם בַּע֑וֹז (oshb:Prov.24.5, 'a wise man is in strength') opens a strength/power image distinct from the house-building figure just closed at 24:4; verse 6 explains that strength through a war-and-counsel figure, כִּ֣י בְ֭תַחְבֻּלוֹת תַּעֲשֶׂה (oshb:Prov.24.6, 'for by strategies you wage war'), the strength/power vocabulary carrying across both verses.
rejected_alternative: Reading 24:5-6 as a continuation of the 24:3-4 house-building cluster was rejected since no building-vocabulary token repeats past verse 4, and the strength/war image opens its own figure at verse 5.
observed_substrate_signals: a strength image opens the pair (Prov.24.5)
a war/counsel motive explains it (Prov.24.6)
device_notes: A second wisdom's-benefit cluster (strength/war) immediately following the house-building cluster, kept separate since the two figures share no token at their seam.

rationale: רָאמ֣וֹת לֶֽאֱוִ֣יל חָכְמ֑וֹת (oshb:Prov.24.7, 'wisdom is too high for a fool') states a complete observation about the fool's exclusion from the gate-council; it shares no root with the strength/war image before it or the scheme/mockery pair after it, so it stands as its own maxim between two clusters.
rejected_alternative: Reading this verse as opening the following scheme/mockery cluster was set aside because the fool and the mocker are named with distinct social-type terms sharing no root across the seam.
observed_substrate_signals: a declarative maxim shares no root with either neighbor (Prov.24.7)
device_notes: Declarative one-verse maxim on the fool's exclusion from public deliberation.

rationale: מְחַשֵּׁ֥ב לְהָרֵ֑עַ (oshb:Prov.24.8, 'one who plots evil') is called מְזִמּ֥וֹת (oshb:Prov.24.8, 'a man of schemes'); verse 9 opens with the same consonantal root, זִמַּ֣ת אִוֶּ֣לֶת (oshb:Prov.24.9, 'the scheme of folly is sin'), the repeated root binding the schemer-maxim to the mocker-maxim that follows it in the same verse.
rejected_alternative: Splitting verse 9 into its own single_proverb was rejected because its opening word repeats verse 8's scheme-root rather than opening an unrelated topic.
observed_substrate_signals: a scheme-root recurs across the seam, at verse 8 and again at verse 9 (Prov.24.8, Prov.24.9)
device_notes: Catchword-bound cluster on the scheming mind, moving from the plotter himself to his plotting's classification as sin.

rationale: הִ֭תְרַפִּיתָ בְּי֥וֹם צָרָ֗ה (oshb:Prov.24.10, 'if you falter in a day of distress, your strength is small') states a complete conditional maxim about personal resilience, sharing no root with the scheming/mockery pair before it or the rescue command after it.
rejected_alternative: Grouping this verse with the rescue command at 24:11-12 was set aside because it addresses the reader's own faltering rather than the reader's duty toward a third party being led to death.
observed_substrate_signals: a conditional maxim on personal resilience shares no root with either neighbor (Prov.24.10)
device_notes: A self-contained conditional maxim, its own topic (personal strength under distress) bridging two unrelated units.

rationale: הַ֭צֵּל לְקֻחִ֣ים לַמָּ֑וֶת (oshb:Prov.24.11, 'rescue those being led away to death') is an imperative command; verse 12 anticipates and answers an excuse, תֹאמַ֗ר...הֲֽלֹא (oshb:Prov.24.12), functioning as the unit's motive by showing that the excuse fails, since God weighs hearts and repays deeds.
rejected_alternative: Reading verse 12 as an independent single_proverb about divine judgment was rejected because its opening clause answers the specific excuse the rescue-command of verse 11 anticipates.
observed_substrate_signals: an imperative command opens the unit (Prov.24.11)
verse 12 rebuts an anticipated excuse rather than opening a new topic (Prov.24.12)
device_notes: Imperative-plus-rebutted-excuse shape, one of the few spots in this span where the motive verse takes the form of an answered objection rather than a plain motive clause.

rationale: A vocative reopens the address, אֱכָל בְּנִ֣י דְבַ֣שׁ (oshb:Prov.24.13, 'eat honey, my son'), after two verses without one; verse 14 applies the honey image to wisdom with כֵּ֤ן דְּעֶ֥ה (oshb:Prov.24.14, 'so know wisdom for your soul') and closes with the hope-not-cut-off clause, וְ֝תִקְוָתְךָ֗ לֹ֣א תִכָּרֵֽת (oshb:Prov.24.14), that recurs, with the same wording, at Prov.23.17-Prov.23.18. A petuchah/pe seg follows verse 14 (oshb:Prov.24.14, single-witness), corroborating the move into the wicked-man warning at 24:15.
rejected_alternative: Reading verse 13 alone as a single_proverb about honey was rejected because its taste-image sets up verse 14's applied purpose clause rather than standing complete on its own.
observed_substrate_signals: a vocative reopens the address (Prov.24.13)
a purpose clause applies the honey image to wisdom (Prov.24.14)
the hope-not-cut-off clause repeats the exact wording of 23:18
petuchah/pe seg closes the unit (Prov.24.14, single-witness)
device_notes: Vocative-plus-applied-purpose shape; the hope refrain shared with 23:18 is texture linking two rows without collapsing either boundary.

rationale: The unit opens right after the petuchah/pe seg at 24:14 (oshb:Prov.24.14, single-witness) with a direct address to a named wrongdoer, אַל תֶּאֱרֹ֣ב רָ֭שָׁע (oshb:Prov.24.15, 'do not lie in wait, wicked one'); verse 16 supplies the motive with כִּ֤י (oshb:Prov.24.16) and the righteous-falls-and-rises antithesis, closing the two-verse unit.
rejected_alternative: Reading verse 16 as a detached single_proverb on the righteous falling seven times was rejected because its motive clause exists to ground the prohibition verse 15 addresses to the wicked man.
observed_substrate_signals: a direct address to the wrongdoer opens the prohibition (Prov.24.15)
a motive clause with the falls-and-rises antithesis follows (Prov.24.16)
petuchah/pe at the immediately preceding verse (Prov.24.14, single-witness)
device_notes: Antithetic motive clause (righteous rises / wicked overthrown) grounding a direct-address prohibition.

rationale: בִּנְפֹ֣ל (oshb:Prov.24.17, 'when...falls') opens a fresh prohibition unrelated to the wicked-man-ambush warning just closed; its object carries a ketiv/qere note, אויביך/אֽ֭וֹיִבְךָ (oshb:Prov.24.17, ketiv/qere, single-witness), before the prohibition itself, אַל תִּשְׂמָ֑ח (oshb:Prov.24.17, 'do not rejoice'); verse 18 supplies the motive with פֶּן (oshb:Prov.24.18, 'lest Yahweh see it and turn his wrath').
rejected_alternative: Merging this pair with the 24:19-20 envy prohibition into one four-verse unit was set aside because a fresh imperative reopens at 24:19 with its own motive rather than continuing this one.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition opens the pair, with a ketiv/qere note at its object (Prov.24.17, single-witness)
a motive clause follows at verse 18 (Prov.24.18)
device_notes: Prohibition-plus-motive shape, the enemy's fall framed as a test of the reader's own character rather than a legal or commercial scene.

rationale: אַל תִּתְחַ֥ר (oshb:Prov.24.19, 'do not fret') opens a doubled prohibition, continued after its object by אַל תְּ֝קַנֵּ֗א (oshb:Prov.24.19, 'do not envy the wicked'); verse 20 supplies the motive with כִּ֤י (oshb:Prov.24.20, 'the evil man's future holds no reward, the wicked man's lamp is snuffed out'). The second verb repeats the chapter's opening prohibition at Prov.24.1, the same root bracketing the chapter's opening unit and this later one without merging them.
rejected_alternative: Reading this pair as a continuation of the 24:17-18 enemy's-fall prohibition was rejected because a fresh doubled imperative reopens at 24:19 rather than extending verse 18's purpose clause.
observed_substrate_signals: a doubled prohibition opens the pair (Prov.24.19)
a motive clause with the snuffed-lamp image follows (Prov.24.20)
the envy-verb recurs from 24:1, bracketing rather than joining the two units
device_notes: The envy-verb frames the chapter's own units (24:1-2 and 24:19-20) at a distance; recorded as texture, not as grounds to widen either row.

rationale: The chapter's closing vocative opens the unit, יְרָֽא אֶת יְהוָ֣ה בְּנִ֣י (oshb:Prov.24.21, 'fear Yahweh, my son') continued by וָמֶ֑לֶךְ (oshb:Prov.24.21, 'and the king'); verse 22 supplies the motive with כִּֽי (oshb:Prov.24.22, 'for their calamity will rise suddenly'). The verse closes the C3 collection, and a setumah/samekh seg sits at this verse (oshb:Prov.24.22, single-witness), the book's one setumah seg total, corroborating at tier-3 the seam this row's own vocative-plus-motive grammar already argues at tier-1.
rejected_alternative: Reading verse 22 as opening the C4 appendix rather than closing this unit was rejected because its motive clause grounds the fear-Yahweh-and-king command of verse 21 rather than introducing the heading that follows.
observed_substrate_signals: a vocative and imperative open the closing unit of C3 (Prov.24.21)
a motive clause closes it (Prov.24.22)
a setumah/samekh seg sits at the closing verse, 1 of 52 parashah segs total (Prov.24.22, single-witness)
device_notes: The collection's final vocative-plus-motive admonition; the setumah seg corroborates without driving the boundary already argued from the grammar.

rationale: גַּם אֵ֥לֶּה (oshb:Prov.24.23, 'also these') opens the C4 appendix immediately after the setumah/samekh seg at 24:22 (oshb:Prov.24.22, single-witness); the heading's own maxim, הַֽכֵּר פָּנִ֖ים בְּמִשְׁפָּ֣ט (oshb:Prov.24.23, 'to show partiality in judgment is not good'), is illustrated by verse 24's case of calling the wicked righteous and resolved by verse 25's adversative, וְלַמּוֹכִיחִ֥ים (oshb:Prov.24.25, 'but to those who convict, it will be pleasant'), the three verses forming one developing statement on judicial partiality rather than a bare header plus two unrelated maxims.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the header at 24:23 into its own row from the illustration at 24:24-25 was considered, on the model of the mishle headers elsewhere, but was set aside because 24:23 already states a complete partiality maxim that 24:24-25 illustrates and resolves rather than merely labels.
observed_substrate_signals: the heading opens with its own complete maxim (Prov.24.23)
an adversative resolves the case at verse 25 (Prov.24.25)
a setumah/samekh seg sits at the immediately preceding verse (Prov.24.22, single-witness)
device_notes: Antithetic close (curse on the partial judge, blessing on the one who convicts) built out from a heading-maxim rather than a plain antithetic couplet.

rationale: שְׂפָתַ֥יִם יִשָּׁ֑ק (oshb:Prov.24.26, 'he kisses the lips') paired with מֵ֝שִׁ֗יב דְּבָרִ֥ים נְכֹחִֽים (oshb:Prov.24.26, 'who gives a right answer') is a self-contained simile about honest speech, sharing no root with the judicial-partiality unit before it or the field-work command after it.
rejected_alternative: Reading this verse as closing the judicial-partiality cluster at 24:23-25 was rejected because its subject moves from courtroom testimony to speech ethics generally, sharing no vocabulary that bridges the seam.
observed_substrate_signals: a kiss-simile shares no root with either neighbor (Prov.24.26)
device_notes: A declarative kiss-simile, a notably compact figure, standing between two units of different topics.

rationale: הָ֘כֵ֤ן בַּח֨וּץ מְלַאכְתֶּ֗ךָ (oshb:Prov.24.27, 'prepare your work outside') issues a sequence of three imperatives about the right order of field-work and house-building, lacking a motive clause; a petuchah/pe seg follows the verse (oshb:Prov.24.27, single-witness).
rejected_alternative: Classifying this verse as an admonition_unit on the strength of its imperative verbs was set aside since it states a priority-ordering maxim rather than developing a command with a supporting motive clause.
observed_substrate_signals: three sequential imperatives on work order lack a motive clause (Prov.24.27)
petuchah/pe seg closes the verse (Prov.24.27, single-witness)
device_notes: A priority-ordering maxim in imperative clothing, matching the pattern used for 22:28 and 23:23.

rationale: אַל תְּהִ֣י עֵד חִנָּ֣ם (oshb:Prov.24.28, 'do not be a witness against your neighbor for nothing') states a complete false-witness maxim lacking a motive clause; it opens right after the petuchah/pe seg at 24:27 (oshb:Prov.24.27, single-witness) and shares no root with the field-work maxim before it or the non-retaliation maxim after it.
rejected_alternative: Grouping this verse with the following non-retaliation maxim at 24:29 as one two-verse unit was rejected since false witness and personal revenge are distinct wrongs, sharing no vocabulary between them.
observed_substrate_signals: a false-witness maxim lacks a motive clause (Prov.24.28)
petuchah/pe at the immediately preceding verse (Prov.24.27, single-witness)
device_notes: A bare imperative maxim on courtroom honesty, its second colon (deceiving with the lips) extending rather than motivating the opening colon.

rationale: אַל תֹּאמַ֗ר (oshb:Prov.24.29, 'do not say') opens a forbidden planned speech-act of revenge, completed by כַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר עָֽשָׂה לִ֭י כֵּ֤ן אֶֽעֱשֶׂה לּ֑וֹ (oshb:Prov.24.29, 'as he did to me so I will do to him'), complete in one verse, lacking a motive clause and sharing no root with the false-witness maxim before it or the sluggard's-field vignette after it.
rejected_alternative: Reading this verse as the opening line of the sluggard's-field unit was set aside because the first-person narrative voice of 24:30 begins a distinct autobiographical frame the revenge-maxim does not share.
observed_substrate_signals: a forbidden revenge-speech maxim lacks a motive clause and shares no root with either neighbor (Prov.24.29)
device_notes: A quoted-speech prohibition (the forbidden words are themselves cited) rather than a plain second-person command.

rationale: A first-person narrative frame opens the span, עַל שְׂדֵ֣ה אִישׁ עָצֵ֣ל עָבַ֑רְתִּי (oshb:Prov.24.30, 'I passed by the field of a lazy man'), distinct from the second-person imperative maxims running through the rest of C4; verses 31-32 continue the observation-and-reflection voice, verse 33 quotes the threefold מְעַ֣ט (oshb:Prov.24.33, 'a little...a little...a little') refrain, and verse 34 closes with the applied consequence in direct second-person address, so your poverty comes as a robber. A petuchah/pe seg closes the span at verse 34 (oshb:Prov.24.34, single-witness), corroborating the close of both this unit and the C4 appendix.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the span into a narrative pair (30-32) and a separate refrain-plus-application pair (33-34) was considered but rejected because the threefold refrain at verse 33 depends on the sluggard the narrative frame introduces rather than standing on its own.
observed_substrate_signals: a first-person narrative frame opens the span (Prov.24.30)
a threefold refrain follows (Prov.24.33)
petuchah/pe seg closes the span and the C4 appendix (Prov.24.34, single-witness)
device_notes: Narrative-observation frame closing in direct second-person application -- the formal shape shared with the wine poem at 23:29-35, here on sloth rather than drink; the span also closes the C4 appendix and the writer part.
